quote: I don't know. I I have no idea what something like that cost. I don't probably can't can't afford it. I'm on a fixed income.
stewart_read: Textbook 'can't afford it' cost objection at the very start; schema flip is 'what you can't afford is your current bill' but rep instead pivots straight to explaining the bill-swap program mechanics.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep could be strategically avoiding an early argument by reassuring with the program pitch first — but the pitch is delivered as features, not as an inversion, so this reads reactive.
coaching_implication: Coach Bucky to use the fixed-income/affordability line as the entry point for the bill-swap flip, not a cue to explain how the program works.

quote: Actually, we have a program called the bill swap. We actually take a look at your power bill, and we, replace it and lower it with a cheaper solar bill.
stewart_read: Rep explains the mechanics of the savings program (guarantee framing, installation/panels) before any qualification has happened — this is closer-tier content delivered unprompted.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be a legitimacy move to keep the customer engaged after her price anxiety — but the content goes beyond reassurance into program mechanics and guarantees.
coaching_implication: Redirect to the specialist for program mechanics; use a shorter reassurance ('that's exactly what we look at with the specialist') and move to verify.

quote: About twenty years. ... He lived here since it was built in 1968, of course, that he died.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a spousal loss tied to the home's history — a trust gift — and rep's response is a generic 'You love your home?' without acknowledging the loss.
coaching_implication: A brief acknowledgment ('sounds like this home means a lot') would have built real rapport instead of skating past a vulnerability disclosure.

quote: around 500 or more, sometimes close to 6.
stewart_read: Bill captured cleanly within the 4-minute target, but the rep's acknowledgment ('We could definitely help with that') is generic and not flipped into alignment-against-the-utility.
coaching_implication: Capture-and-move-on failure pattern; rep should reflect the $500-600 figure back later when setting the appointment to create urgency.

quote: Right. And that says my bill is 25.69% higher than last year, the March.
stewart_read: Customer hands the rep a live, self-discovered anchor (bill up 25.69% year over year) and rep's response is a flat 'Oh, good thing we're calling' non-sequitur that doesn't build on it.
coaching_implication: This was a gift-wrapped urgency moment; rep should have tied it directly to the appointment pitch ('that's exactly the trend the specialist will show you how to stop').

quote: Then you have a credit score over 6 70?
stewart_read: Customer doesn't know her score; rep resolves with 'Okay. We'll just say yes' — a soft pass-through rather than a real qualification, consistent with the schema's note that stated credit is unreliable.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be intentional per Spencer's operator note that closer's pull should decide, not the setter — in which case this is correct procedure, not a gap.
coaching_implication: Flag for Kenny's policy resolution on stated-vs-pulled credit; as written this is an ungrounded pass rather than a documented protocol.

quote: the only thing they ask because you're able to access your email, and you're not driving.
stewart_read: Button-up is garbled — no_driving and computer-access elements are mashed into one confusing sentence, and there's no clean 'is that fair?' handshake before hanging up.
coaching_implication: Slow down the button-up script; deliver the no-driving/computer line cleanly and close with an explicit fairness check.
